section_summary: This section is dominated by appeals from citizens, clergy, educators, peace organizations, and Chinese correspondents urging the Roosevelt administration to embargo arms, oil, scrap metal, and other strategic exports to Japan. State Department replies explain the constraints of the Neutrality Act, congressional inaction, the voluntary restriction of aircraft exports, and procedures for seeking compensation for Japanese occupation of American property in China. The section also contains reports and statistical studies of Japan’s strategic-material imports, accounts of Japanese bombing at Chengdu, advocacy clippings, and correspondence revealing the policies of American industrial exporters.

subfiles.title: Closing portion of Myra Vaughn’s embargo appeal
subfiles.about: Vaughn asks what action citizens should take to secure an embargo on goods shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving conclusion says that many letters and telegrams have been sent urging an embargo on goods to Japan until the conflict ends. Vaughn asks for a course of action through which citizens can make their views effective.

subfiles.title: Reply to Myra Vaughn concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles explains the administration’s policy on war-material and aircraft exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the export statement and 1937 arms proclamation, cites disapproval of aircraft supplies to forces bombing civilians, and says no arms or aircraft licenses for Japan were issued in the first half of 1939.

subfiles.title: Dow W. Harter transmits Florence Fitch’s letter
subfiles.about: Harter forwards a constituent’s appeal about American supplies to Japan and requests help drafting a reply.
subfiles.summary: Representative Harter sends Oberlin professor Florence Fitch's letter and asks Hull to help with an answer.

subfiles.title: Florence M. Fitch urges action against arming Japan
subfiles.about: Fitch urges Congress to stop American support for Japan’s war in China before adjournment.
subfiles.summary: Fitch, with experience in China and Japan, condemns Japan's assault and says Congress must act before adjourning.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Dow W. Harter
subfiles.about: Hull supplies a departmental statement for answering Florence Fitch’s protest.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Harter’s letter and offers a statement on war-material exports for possible transmission to Fitch. He repeats the policy discouraging aircraft exports to forces bombing civilians and notes the absence of licensed arms and aircraft exports to Japan during the first six months of 1939.

subfiles.title: Suggested paragraph concerning Olson’s Shanghai property
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes language directing Hilda Olson to the American consul general regarding Japanese occupation of property in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Suggested reply assumes Olson's organization took its Shanghai property problem to the consul general, who will assist.

subfiles.title: Hilda Olson appeals for an embargo and protection of medical-college property
subfiles.about: Olson urges an embargo on munitions and credit to Japan and asks about property occupied after the evacuation of her Shanghai medical college.
subfiles.summary: Olson describes the 1937 evacuation of the Woman's Christian Medical College, argues ending munitions and credit would halt the killing, and asks Hull to work for peace.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green replies to Hilda Olson
subfiles.about: Green explains the Neutrality Act and advises Olson to seek consular help concerning the Shanghai property.
subfiles.summary: Green says the Neutrality Act requires an arms embargo on both belligerents after a war finding, not a one-sided embargo; repeats the aircraft policy and no Japan arms licenses; the consul general can assist.

subfiles.title: Reported resumption of Indochinese iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Peter H. A. Flood, American Consul at Saigon
subfiles.about: Flood reports authorization for renewed shipments of iron ore from French Indochina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Domei report in L’Avenir du Tonkin says the governor-general authorized the export of 10,000 tons of iron ore despite a 1938 restriction. Flood supplies statistics showing a rapid rise to 89,227 metric tons in 1938, more than 95 percent of Indochina’s iron-ore exports.

subfiles.title: Secretary’s instruction to prepare a reply
subfiles.about: The Secretary directs Hamilton to prepare a draft reply for signature.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten instruction assigning Hamilton to prepare a reply, apparently to Bishop Hobson's correspondence.

subfiles.title: Bishop Henry W. Hobson urges an end to war-material traffic with Japan
subfiles.about: Hobson reports overwhelming public and church opposition to American shipments sustaining Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Hobson says people throughout the eastern United States regard the trade as immoral support for Japanese aggression. He reports unanimous action by the Diocese of Southern Ohio and urges Hull and Congress to act during the current session.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bishop Henry W. Hobson
subfiles.about: Hull explains the status of embargo bills and the Department’s existing export policy.
subfiles.summary: Hull says several bills covering arms, scrap iron, oil, and other materials are pending but are not expected to receive action in the current congressional session. He encloses his July 21 Senate letter and the Department’s export statement and reiterates the aircraft policy and licensing figures.

subfiles.title: Suggested clarification of consular assistance to Olson
subfiles.about: The memorandum clarifies what the American consul general can do for the Woman’s Christian Medical College.
subfiles.summary: Proposed paragraph: the consul can help prepare a damage claim, submit it to Japan and seek the property's return, citing precedents.

subfiles.title: Hilda Olson’s renewed appeal after the Chengdu bombing
subfiles.about: Olson quotes eyewitness reports of Japanese bombing at Chengdu and renews demands for an embargo on strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: Olson reports bombs hitting West China Union University after the Chengdu raid, killing a student, argues American oil and scrap enable the raids, and explains fears that filing a Shanghai property claim could expose staff to retaliation.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost replies to Hilda Olson’s renewed appeal
subfiles.about: Yost explains the statutory limits on export controls and clarifies the consular claims procedure.
subfiles.summary: Yost says law covers defined arms, tin-plate scrap and helium, so Congress must legislate for scrap iron and oil; embargo bills failed; the Shanghai consul can help obtain damages without implying a state of war.

subfiles.title: Lincoln Y. Wang appeals to Roosevelt for an export prohibition
subfiles.about: Wang asks Roosevelt to prevent American arms and aircraft from supporting Japanese aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: Wang contrasts American democratic ideals with Japan’s invasion and the suffering of China. He denounces merchants who profit from weapons and aircraft exports, rejects isolationism, and urges a moral international policy grounded in peace and justice.

subfiles.title: Conversation with the Boston embargo delegation
subfiles.about: State Department officials discuss the Pittman Resolution with representatives of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression.
subfiles.summary: Boston embargo delegation reports thousands of signatures; Sayre directs it to Congress and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and cites treaty sanctity when asked about the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Eleanor Brooks Fabyan requests an appointment
subfiles.about: Fabyan introduces an anti-aggression delegation and asks Sayre for a brief meeting.
subfiles.summary: Fabyan identifies herself through Bryn Mawr and international-relations connections and describes a New England petition bearing more than 10,000 signatures against shipments of war supplies to Japan. She sketches the backgrounds of proposed delegates, including Lewis Dexter and Gabriel Lasker, and asks for a few minutes of Sayre’s time.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Roger Greene’s presidential correspondence
subfiles.about: Green records the drafting and White House transmission of a reply to Roger S. Greene.
subfiles.summary: Memo: the Department drafted a presidential reply to Roger Greene's July 21 letter at General Watson's request, sent to the White House July 28.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene urges Roosevelt to support an embargo
subfiles.about: Greene argues that restricting strategic exports to Japan would weaken Japan and improve the international balance against Germany.
subfiles.summary: Greene seeks limits on petroleum, metals, vehicles, and metalworking machinery and argues that Britain would probably cooperate. He dismisses the danger of Japanese retaliation, connects Japan’s weakness on Russia’s rear to German caution, and urges Roosevelt to encourage congressional supporters before adjournment.

subfiles.title: Draft presidential reply to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: The draft acknowledges Greene’s views on neutrality legislation and strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: Draft presidential reply notes Greene's campaign to restrict petroleum, metals, vehicles and machinery exports to Japan and encloses July 1939 State statements.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to file 893.34/599
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers from decimal file 894.24/696 to 893.34/599.
subfiles.summary: Single-line cross-reference to file 893.34/599.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction to acknowledge a letter
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hamilton to acknowledge the following correspondence on his behalf.
subfiles.summary: The brief instruction assigns Hamilton the preparation of an acknowledgment. It relates to the ensuing letter from F. E. Hyslop.

subfiles.title: F. E. Hyslop criticizes policy toward Japan
subfiles.about: Hyslop welcomes termination of the Japanese commercial treaty but demands immediate application of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Hyslop criticizes refusing to recognize a state of war in China, arguing the treaty delays raw material restrictions but not a munitions embargo.

subfiles.title: Maxwell Hamilton replies to F. E. Hyslop
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Hyslop’s criticism and summarizes the Department’s export policy.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says Hyslop’s views and enclosed editorial have been noted and supplies the standard statement on exports to China and Japan. He repeats the Department’s opposition to aircraft supplies used in bombing civilians and welcomes Hyslop’s approval of the July 26 notice terminating the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Data relating to a suggested embargo on war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum quantifies Japan’s reliance on American strategic materials and estimates the likely effects of an embargo.
subfiles.summary: The study analyzes Senator Pittman’s proposal and recommends adding copper and automobiles to the listed arms, iron, steel, scrap, oil, and gasoline. A table compares 1937 and 1938 exports and supplier shares, showing particularly heavy Japanese dependence on the United States for aircraft, scrap metal, petroleum, copper, and automobiles. Commodity sections conclude that an embargo would create growing military and economic inefficiency but that Japanese stocks, domestic production, and alternate suppliers would prevent an immediate collapse.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s request for a reply to Bogert
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hamilton to draft an appropriate answer to the following letter.
subfiles.summary: Office instruction sending H. L. Bogert's appeal on China and the Nine-Power Pact to Hamilton for drafting.

subfiles.title: H. L. Bogert urges fulfillment of the Nine-Power Pact
subfiles.about: Bogert praises treaty termination but argues that American exports make the United States complicit in Japan’s violation of Chinese sovereignty.
subfiles.summary: Bogert contends that shipments of oil, gasoline, and scrap iron contradict the spirit of the Nine-Power Pact commitment to China’s independence and territorial integrity. He asks Welles to use available governmental powers to help drive Japan from China and end American complicity.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to H. L. Bogert
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges Bogert’s protest and reviews unsuccessful embargo bills and aircraft-export policy.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that Congress failed to enact proposed restrictions on arms, scrap iron, oil, and other war-useful articles. He encloses the Department’s export statement and again emphasizes voluntary compliance with its discouragement of aircraft supplies for forces bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Western Pennsylvania Committee appeal to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: McKee proposes voluntary agreements against war-material exports to Japan during the treaty’s six-month notice period.
subfiles.summary: McKee welcomes abrogation of the Japanese trade treaty but regrets that exports can continue during the waiting period. He encloses religious statements and corporate correspondence, proposes voluntary agreements backed by publicity, and notes manufacturers’ concern that Japanese demand is raising scrap prices.

subfiles.title: Clipping: U.S. plane sold to Japan Air Transport
subfiles.about: The clipping reports the sale of a Douglas DC-4 to Japan Air Transport.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: a US plane sold to Japan Air Transport, favored by officials as strengthening production capacity, at $725,000.

subfiles.title: On the Record: “The Summer and the President—American Foreign Policy,” opening portion
subfiles.about: Thompson criticizes the incoherence of American foreign policy and congressional neutrality.
subfiles.summary: Thompson's column contrasts stated Open Door and treaty commitments with absent policy, discussing fascist economic penetration and arguing American isolation is untenable.

subfiles.title: Bishop Lucey assails isolation and blind neutrality
subfiles.about: Bishop Lucey argues that isolation and neutrality toward aggression violate Catholic moral teaching.
subfiles.summary: Bishop Lucey, citing Pope Benedict XV, urges arbitration and sanctions against militaristic states, calls neutrality in the face of aggression immoral, and cites Ethiopia, China and Bohemia.

subfiles.title: Editorial: “Does Japan Understand Now?”
subfiles.about: The editorial welcomes denunciation of the 1911 treaty and demands an embargo on war-making materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorial treats treaty termination as a response to Japanese mistreatment of Americans in China, condemns scrap-iron and machinery exports as 'blood money' and urges investigating the Boston firms.

subfiles.title: Participation in Aggression: religious leaders’ declaration
subfiles.from: G. Ashton Oldham and other religious leaders
subfiles.to: American public and congressional foreign-relations committees
subfiles.about: The declaration calls on religious groups and governments to end economic support for aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: Two hundred religious leaders say supplying aggressors spreads war, with six principles opposing aggressive war and injustice and favoring stronger peace machinery.

subfiles.title: Shareholder inquiry to Bethlehem Steel
subfiles.about: McKee asks whether Bethlehem Steel products are being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McKee, a shareholder, argues Americans should not build up an aggressor and believes most shareholders would sacrifice Japanese profits.

subfiles.title: Bethlehem Steel reply concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: McMath confirms substantial Bethlehem Steel sales to Japan but rejects unilateral corporate restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Bethlehem Steel says it shipped substantial standard steel products to Japan in 1937-1938, that competitors would otherwise make the sales, and that restrictions should come from the national government.

subfiles.title: Atlantic Refining Company reply concerning Japan
subfiles.about: Atlantic Refining states that none of its products are being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The company directly answers McKee’s inquiry in the negative. No explanation or qualification accompanies the response.

subfiles.title: Gulf Oil Corporation reply concerning Japanese business
subfiles.about: Gulf Oil acknowledges regular but limited exports to Japan and intends to continue them.
subfiles.summary: Gulf Oil says Japan is a satisfactory low-risk market served by a broker, minimizes its trade versus competitors, and says regular requirements will continue.

subfiles.title: Texas Gulf Sulphur Company reply concerning Japan
subfiles.about: The company states that it has never shipped its products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Texas Gulf Sulphur categorically denies current or past shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Union Carbide reply concerning sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Union Carbide describes its Japanese sales as small quantities of industrial carbon products and chemicals.
subfiles.summary: Union Carbide says sales to Japan are limited to carbon products and organic chemicals and commercially insignificant.

subfiles.title: United Aircraft reply concerning sales to Japan
subfiles.about: United Aircraft acknowledges intermittent Japanese purchases, including one airplane.
subfiles.summary: United Aircraft says it sold products to Japan over twelve years, including one airplane years earlier.

subfiles.title: International Nickel Company reply concerning Japanese sales
subfiles.about: The company acknowledges worldwide nickel sales including Japan while arguing that most nickel serves peaceful industry.
subfiles.summary: International Nickel says it shares the wish to prevent war use but finds it nearly unattainable since most nickel goes to ordinary industry.

subfiles.title: Western Pennsylvania Committee appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: McKee asks Roosevelt to seek voluntary restrictions on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This presidential version closely parallels McKee’s letter to Hull, praising treaty abrogation while criticizing continued exports during the notice period. It proposes informal agreements and publicity to bring manufacturers into line and points to rising scrap prices as a concern for independent steel producers.

subfiles.title: On the Record: “The Summer and the President—American Foreign Policy,” continuation
subfiles.about: The continuation assesses unilateral sanctions against Japan and the wider consequences of isolationism.
subfiles.summary: Thompson argues an embargo alone would inconvenience Japan, leave loopholes and might push it toward the Axis; she links Far East, Monroe Doctrine and European crisis.

subfiles.title: Duplicate opening of “Bishop Lucey Assails ‘Isolation,’ ‘Blind Neutrality’”
subfiles.about: This duplicate opening repeats Lucey’s case against isolation and morally neutral foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate opening of Bishop Lucey's address invoking the papal peace program, arbitration, sanctions and Roosevelt's quarantine proposal.
